content: Intergovernmental organizations, such as the World Health Organization (WHO), play a significant role in supporting research by providing both funding and technical assistance. This support is delivered through programs at their headquarters as well as through regional offices. WHO has specialized research programs that focus on areas such as reproductive health and tropical diseases. The not-for-profit private sector also contributes to research funding, with several foundations, both large and small, actively involved. Examples include the Wellcome Trust in the UK and the Rockefeller, Ford, and Bill and Melinda Gates Foundations in the USA. In the for-profit private sector, pharmaceutical companies, primarily based in industrialized countries, are increasingly investing substantial amounts of money in research and development. An intermediary layer often acts as a bridge between funders and researchers, facilitating the flow of resources and support. A growing number of international research programs are focusing on specific areas of health research. Examples include the Population Council headquartered in New York, Family Health International (FHI) based in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, and the Program for Appropriate Technology in Health (PATH) headquartered in Seattle. Funding organizations receive far more research proposals than they can fund, making the selection process highly competitive. Several factors are typically considered when deciding whether to fund a proposal. These include the importance and relevance of the research question to the agency’s stated interests, the quality of the research design, the investigators’ ability to execute the project, the capacity of the research facility, the institution’s ability to manage administrative and financial procedures, ethical considerations, a realistic and justifiable budget, a reasonable timeframe for project completion, an understanding of potential challenges, and the clarity and style of the written proposal. Writing with enthusiasm is encouraged, but exaggerations should be avoided. Funding organizations use various mechanisms to select and fund research projects. These include soliciting proposals directly from specific institutions, advertising and inviting proposals in areas of interest, or maintaining an open-door policy for any good proposal. When soliciting proposals, funding agencies often approach centers of excellence and request submissions in specific areas of importance. In competitive processes, proposals are independently reviewed and scored, with a small number selected for funding. Some agencies may first request a brief concept outline before shortlisting applications and asking for full proposals from the shortlisted candidates. For open-door policies, it is advisable to send a brief outline of the project and the funding level requested to gauge the agency’s interest before submitting a full proposal. Most funding organizations have websites where information about their interests and funding mechanisms can be accessed. Research proposals are commonly subjected to peer review, and reviewers may suggest revisions to improve the proposal’s acceptability. Investigators should address these criticisms where possible and justify any decisions not to adopt suggested changes. It is helpful to provide a separate page indicating the criticisms made and how the revised proposal responds to them. A research proposal typically follows a standard format, which includes components of the research protocol along with additional information. Some funding agencies have their own standardized formats to streamline the review process. The components of a research proposal include a title page, project summary, project description, ethical considerations, gender issues, timetable, anticipated problems, budget, references, and the curriculum vitae (CV) of the investigators. The title page should include the project title, principal investigator(s), institution, project duration, and the funding requested. Research grants are usually awarded to institutions rather than individuals, so the institution’s name should be included. If the institution is unfamiliar to the agency, brief information about it may be provided as an annex. The name of the financial officer responsible for administering the grant should also be included. The project duration must be specified, as most agencies do not commit support beyond three years. For multi-year projects, the funding requested for each year should be outlined. The project summary should be carefully written, as it is often the first and sometimes the only part read by reviewers. It should persuasively highlight the importance and strengths of the project. The project description should follow the research protocol and explain the rationale for the project, its importance, and its relevance to the funding agency’s interests. Previous work by the investigators on the research topic and any pilot studies conducted should be included to demonstrate feasibility and competence. Ethical considerations must be fully addressed in the proposal. Approval from the local ethics review committee does not absolve the donor agency or the research institution of their ethical responsibilities. Gender issues should also be addressed, as many funding organizations are increasingly conscious of these concerns. The investigators should commit to a timetable, including preparatory phases, data collection, final analysis, and report writing. For long-duration projects, milestones should be set and progress reports reviewed by the funding agency. Funding is often released based on these progress reports. Investigators should demonstrate awareness of potential obstacles and explain how they would address them. A lack of anticipated problems may indicate insufficient planning. The budget should be itemized and justified, with categories such as personnel, equipment, supplies, patient care costs, travel, data processing, communications, secretarial expenses, and publication/dissemination costs. Each item will be closely scrutinized to ensure it is necessary and justified. Unrealistic budgets, whether overestimated or underestimated, are likely to lead to proposal rejection. Investigators should limit project objectives to what can realistically be achieved with the requested funds. References should include recent and relevant citations to support the proposal. The CVs of the investigators should be attached to demonstrate their ability to carry out the project. Preliminary studies or other work done by the investigators on the subject should also be included. Scientific rigor is essential in research. This includes adherence to the study protocol, compliance with ethical standards, meticulous record-keeping, objective measurement methods, appropriate statistical analysis, and ongoing familiarity with the literature. Results should be presented in a way that allows other investigators to replicate the study and confirm or refute the findings. Pre-testing the protocol, often through a pilot study, is advisable, especially for large and expensive studies. This helps identify and address logistical and practical problems before the main study begins. The pilot study can also test recruitment methods, measurement tools, and data management systems, ensuring the feasibility and reliability of the research.
